Writing // One

Why video games are the ultimate form of art

The forms that came before this one ask you to sit still. A painting hangs and waits. A novel lets you put it down without noticing. The work hap­pens on one side of the glass and you stand on the other, and the whole tra­di­tion of cri­ti­cism we in­her­ited is a tra­di­tion of de­scrib­ing what goes on over there.

Games moved the glass by making the thing you do the thing the work is about. Interactivity on its own does not manage it: a museum kiosk is interactive and it stays a kiosk. The rules are the medium. A game speaks through what it lets you try and what it charges you to keep going.

That is easy to nod at and hard to hold, because holding it means giving up the habit of looking for the art in whichever parts resemble the older forms. The art is in the rules. The score and the cutscene are the parts that survive being described, which is most of why they get described.

The rules are the sentence

Consider a jump. In one game it is generous: the ledge grabs you and the timing forgives. In an­other it is ex­act, and a frame early is a frame wasted. Neither is the bet­ter jump. They are two dif­fer­ent claims about what ef­fort is worth, and you take the claim in through your hands in­side ninety seconds, long be­fore any­one in the game has said a word.

Change the number of frames a player gets to correct that jump and you have changed the argument the game is making, which is a different edit from changing how hard it is. One version says the world will meet you halfway; the other says it will not, and that any meeting is yours to arrange. There is no equi­val­ent edit any­where else. You can­not make a film eight per cent more for­giv­ing.

That is au­thor­ship at a level the other forms can­not reach. A film can show you a man who is tired. A game can make you tired, and then ask you to do the thing any­way, and the gap between watch­ing resig­na­tion and feel­ing it is the whole dis­tance between sym­pathy and know­ledge.

A film can show you a man who is tired. A game can make you tired, and then ask you to do the thing any­way.

The other forms, contained

It is also the form that holds the others without shrinking them. A game has architecture in it, and performance, and writing that would survive on the page. Cinema ab­sorbed pho­to­graphy and theatre the same way, and we spent a cen­tury call­ing that the great syn­thesis. Games absorbed cinema. They did it while the culture pages were looking somewhere else, because the early ones were ugly and the marketing pointed at children.

Architecture is the one worth staying on, because games did more than borrow it. A level is a building you come to understand by moving through it, which is how you understand a building. Photographs of architecture are useless and plans are worse. A well-made level teaches you its shape the way a house teaches you its shape: by mak­ing you walk it twice.

The dismissals were about legitimacy rather than quality: who gets to say a thing is serious. That question settles itself by attrition, because the people who grew up inside a form become the people who decide. It happened to the novel, which was trash for a century. It happened to television twice.

What it costs

None of this is free. The form's great strength, that you are the one act­ing, is also what makes it the hard­est thing to au­thor. Give a reader a sen­tence and they read the sen­tence. Give a player a room and they will stand in the corner for four minutes look­ing at a bucket. A choice you hand over is a choice you no longer con­trol, and most games an­swer that by hand­ing over al­most noth­ing that mat­ters.

The good ones design for it. They accept that somebody they will not meet finishes the work, in a session they will not see, and they build something sturdy enough to survive that and specific enough to still mean something afterwards. It is a harder brief than a film, and when it lands there is noth­ing else like it.

There is a second cost, and it is the one the form has been slow­est to face. A game has to be played to be met, and play­ing takes hours, some­times tens of them. That is a real bar­rier and it is not snob­bery to say so. A novel asks the same and gets away with it be­cause the cul­ture settled long ago that the ask­ing was worth it. Games are still mak­ing that case, one piece at a time, and they will be mak­ing it for a while yet.

The ceiling

That is the argument. At their ceiling, games do something the older forms cannot do at all. Plenty of games fall short of the older forms, and the ceiling is what we measure an art form by. You do not judge the novel by the airport paperback.

And the ceil­ing keeps mov­ing, which is the part that ought to in­terest any­one who makes things. The medium is fifty years old. People are still inventing its grammar, most of them people who would not describe themselves as inventing a grammar. We are some­where around the 1910s of this thing. We have already had a few films.

I wrote this in March 2025 and filed it under essays and craft. Nine minutes at a reading pace.
